Done. Merged into one if statement.

Right, we don't need these lines. Removed.

Addressed the changes. Combined into a single map `MctpRequester::activeRequests`. A new `Request` struct is introduced to encapsulate the callbacks, timers and other request related data.

Do we need this here?

This was the entry point for the "polling" routine. The only thing that asyncRecv does is queue up the next async read on the socket. Whenever the recv completes (with/without errors) it queues up the next async read and hence basically polls the socket for the received messages. But now due to changes to the implementation this has been removed. And now we are enqueuing a recv for each message we send out.
Done
Why static?

As we are just peeking into the message this buffer isn't really used to read the data. Hence, the buffer is made static in order to avoid redundant creation of a new vector for each asyncRecv call. But with the current change as we are enqueuing multiple receive on the socket I have made the tmp buffer non-static.
Done
Why do you have to processPendingRequests() and asyncRecv() in all the error paths? Seems prone to being missed out if additional error patha are added...
Cleaned up.
Done

This function calls asyncRecv() and asyncRecv() calls this function... I think we need a better pattern (RAII-like) instead of the repititive processPendingRequests() and asyncRecv() calls. Or, why not call asyncRecv() only after sending a message?
Done. Now we are enqueuing a recv for each message we send out.

How did you test ensuring a new request is held when there is a pending one? Can we add unit tests?
Done. Unit tests have been added.
Aren't all of these requirements already implemented in the kernel bindings?

@akurdunkar@nvidia.com you need to do some rephrasing here. What you are handling here is to make sure there is only one outstanding request message to a GPU device implementing the VDM protocol, as that is a VDM protocol restriction (and not an MCTP restriction).

Handling out of order packets/messages, sending to the correct recipient etc. is MCTP scope and handled by the kernel. You are not doing any of these here, so simplify the commit message to match the code.

> Handling out of order packets/messages, sending to the correct recipient etc. is MCTP scope and handled by the kernel. You are not doing any of these here, so simplify the commit message to match the code.

The commit message mentions out-of-order responses and not packets. That, and all the other conditions, are part of the scope of MctpRequester. Conditions 1 and 3 were already handled. Only second condition wasn't handled in the code. 

The excerpt (marked by ''') is from The VDM protocol spec. I have kept it as it is in the updated commit message to provide context. I have added more explanation for condition 2 in the commit message.

Sorry about that — I will run the CI locally first before pushing next time.

Lets use composition here.  We're adding one field, it's not clear that inheritance helps us in this case.

There was a confusion with the earlier implementation as the fields were misplaced. The Request struct was carrying the timeout + callback related context for each request. The intention of having a Request struct was for it to hold the bare-minimum data (msgtype + the actual byte array) required for communication. The OcpVdmRequest will extend the Request struct and should hold the OCP VDM specific context (timeout + response callback + ocp instance id). If we want to use composition instead of inheritance the nomenclature around the OcpVdmRequest and the Request Queues in the Requester becomes a little awkward. I think with the recent patchset (26) the extension of OcpVdmRequest from Request makes more sense (I have properly defined the fields in the correct structs).
Done
I think the commit message should talk about just this detail, not sure we need everything above.
Done
Specify what meta layer, what patches.
Done
Let's avoid introducing new abstractions and concept unless absolutely necessary. Would like to see clear/concise diffs first for introducing queueing in MCTPRequester.

I have simplified the change in the new patchset. The changes are made to the MctpRequester itself. Some Template parameters (and a related concept of a socket) are still required for the Tests, hence have been preserved. The public facing API hasn't changed.

I would like to see diffs to existing MCTPRequester, filename changes and introducing the new Requester class can come in later in a different commit.

Also, I am not sure we need the Requester abstraction. We will support only the kernel MCTP stack.
Done
I am not sure we need this. See comment elsewhere.
Removed.
We are no longer using the implementation from patchset 27.

in my mind, there's no reason to mix together queuing and the request response cycle. We should be able to keep mctprequester in its current (much improved) form and have the queueing stuff just deal with queueing and calling back to the client. It can hand an internal callback to the mctprequester and deal with when to tell mctprequester to do its thing. When its contract to the client is satisfied, it will call the "top level callback" to the client saying "done".
I have addressed this by introducing a QueuingRequester that wraps around the Requester class. More details in the commit message.

let me know if below sequence is valid one 

First request to EID1:
async_wait is set up for first response
No response comes from EID1
Second request to EID2:
Another async_wait is set up for second response
Response comes from EID2
Problem:
The first async_wait will be triggered by the EID2 response
It will read the message and call the callback with EID2
The callback will check the EID and drop the message
But the second async_wait is still pending and might never get the response


Is this a problem or handled is some other way ?

This is not a problem. For each send there's a corresponding recv work that is queued up. This is done in order to ensure that there's always an async recv pending for every request sent. The async recv handler is agnostic of the request context in which it was scheduled/queued as it checks for the right request metadata and then invokes the corresponding callback.
any limit on max outstanding pending requests ?
There's no limit as such, we should be able to handle as many requests as many are queued up.
nit - rename vec to data or something similar.
No longer using this implementation.
Looks simple and clean. Can +1 after retest.

For whatever reasin if the EID didn't exist in the map, what'll happen is a slient insertion with an empty callback? If so, I think it's better to use at() and let an exception be thrown in case the eid didn't exist in the map.
Done
I don't understand why we need activeRequestContexts. We can just keep this in the requestContextQueue until we get called back from Requester...

This was done to solve the issue where the first request for each command wasn't getting queued and back-to-back requests were sent to the GPU with the implementation where we keep the active request context in the queue. Also there's no explicit way to track an active request with that implementation; `activeRequestContexts` helps provide that.

Better to use an std::bind_front instead of lambda here to align with guidelines and how we've done this in the rest of the patches. You could bind a private method just like Requester::handleSendMsgCompletion.
Guideline is https://github.com/openbmc/docs/blob/master/anti-patterns.md#very-long-lambda-callbacks
Done. Using std::bind_front now to call the member function `handleResult`.
at() is almost universally incorrect in an async reactor.
fix all uses of at(), then this LGTM.
uncaught exception.  Use find.
Done. Now the MctpRequester checks if the completionCallbacks contains the callback for the eid.
same here.
Done
Nit, please use vector, or boost devector to avoid mallocs in the hot path.
How will a vector/devector help in avoiding allocations? Are you saying that maybe we already reserve a size of max instance ids in the vector?

> How will a vector/devector help in avoiding allocations?

devector/vector retain memory, and allocate at power of 2 sizes as needed, so in general the only allocation will be the first round of sensor updates.

> Are you saying that maybe we already reserve a size of max instance ids in the vector?

no, reserve is not required here (unless we know exactly how many requests can be in flight), just let the implementation handle it.
Done, using a devector now.
Keeping these in a seperate data structure can lead to use after free issues.

Not sure if I get this. We need `RequestContext` in order to store the queued request's buffers. As the lifetime of these buffers is the responsibility of the caller, how will the use after free issues will be seen?
Span is a pointer to memory.  It will generally be seen on startup/shutdown/reinit. RequestContext should maintain its own buffers (probably vector of char/uint8).

But if the requester makes a copy of the message wouldn't that defeat the point of passing in just the view to the request buffer? Currently each sensor has preallocated request and response buffers and we are just passing the view of it to the requester.
It is guarenteed that the request response buffers will be available for the lifetime of the request-response transaction.
pass by rvalue reference &&
As we are already moving the callback function (with std::move) while creating the RequestContext not sure why we need to pass it as an rvalue reference explicitly
Because it prevents an extra move constructor.  This is a nit.
Done, passing by rvalue reference now.
